- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. 1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Add view transitions with an agent 16 17 The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 18 19 Install the skill: 20 21 ```bash filename="Terminal" 22 npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 23 ``` 24 25 Then prompt the agent with something like: 26 27 ```prompt 28 Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 29 ``` 30 31 Or prompt for a specific transition, such as: 32 33 - Morphing a thumbnail into a hero image 34 - Sliding between routes forward and back 35 - Crossfading content within the same route 36 37 To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. 38 39 ## Example 40 41 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 42 43 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 44 45 You can find the resources used in this example here: 46 47 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 48 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 49 50 View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. The App Router uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which contain all stable React 19 changes as well as newer features like `ViewTransition`. You do not need to install `react@canary` yourself. 51 52 > [!NOTE] 53 > React's integration uses newer View Transitions API features (transition types and `view-transition-class`), available in Chromium 125+ and recent Safari and Firefox versions. Some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally; the transitions do not animate. 54 55 Import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 56 57 ```tsx 58 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 59 ``` 60 61 `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 62 63 ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 64 65 The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 66 67 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 68 69 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 70 71 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 72 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 73 import Image from 'next/image' 74 import Link from 'next/link' 75 76 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 77 return ( 78
79 {photos.map((photo) => ( 80 81 82 83 84 85 ))} 86
87 ) 88 } 89 ``` 90 91 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 92 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 93 import Image from 'next/image' 94 95 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 96 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 97 98 return ( 99 100
101 102
103 104 ) 105 } 106 ``` 107 108 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 109 110 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 111 112 The morph plays when the destination content renders in the same commit as the navigation, which is the case with prefetched (cached) pages. If the destination suspends into a fallback first, no pair forms, and the content animates with its enter animation instead when it arrives. 113 114 #### Customizing the morph animation 115 116 The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"` together with `default="none"`. The `share` prop assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 117 118 ```tsx 119 120 121 122 ``` 123 124 Add the same props to both Step 1 snippets (`photo-grid.tsx` and `photo-content.tsx`). `default="none"` keeps each named image from running its own crossfade on every unrelated transition. Without it, every named `` animates whenever any transition runs on the page. When you add `default="none"` to a named pair, keep the explicit `share`. With `default="none"` and no `share` prop, the pair silently stops morphing. 125 126 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 127 ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 128 animation-duration: 400ms; 129 } 130 ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 131 animation-name: via-blur; 132 } 133 @keyframes via-blur { 134 30% { 135 filter: blur(3px); 136 } 137 } 138 ``` 139 140 The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 141 142 ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 143 144 The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 145 146 Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 147 148 In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 149 150 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 151 152 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 153 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 154 155 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 156 const { id } = await params 157 158 return ( 159 162 163 164 } 165 > 166 167 168 169 170 ) 171 } 172 ``` 173 174 As in Step 1, `default="none"` prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph. 175 176 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 177 178 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 179 :root { 180 --duration-exit: 150ms; 181 --duration-enter: 210ms; 182 --duration-move: 400ms; 183 } 184 185 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 186 animation: 187 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 188 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 189 } 190 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 191 animation: 192 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 193 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 194 } 195 196 @keyframes fade { 197 from { 198 filter: blur(3px); 199 opacity: 0; 200 } 201 to { 202 filter: blur(0); 203 opacity: 1; 204 } 205 } 206 @keyframes slide-y { 207 from { 208 transform: translateY(10px); 209 } 210 to { 211 transform: translateY(0); 212 } 213 } 214 ``` 215 216 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 217 218 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 219 220 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 221 222 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 223 224 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 225 226 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 227 228 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 229 230 {/* photo thumbnail */} 231 232 ``` 233 234 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 235 236 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 237 238 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 239 240 ← Gallery 241 242 ``` 243 244 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 245 246 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 247 248 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 249 262 {/* page content */} 263 264 ``` 265 266 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 267 268 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 269 270 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 271 284 285 286 ``` 287 288 The CSS for directional slides: 289 290 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 291 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: -60px; 293 animation: 294 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 296 } 297 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 298 --slide-offset: 60px; 299 animation: 300 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 301 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 302 } 303 304 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: 60px; 306 animation: 307 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 309 } 310 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 311 --slide-offset: -60px; 312 animation: 313 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 314 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 315 } 316 317 @keyframes slide { 318 from { 319 translate: var(--slide-offset); 320 } 321 to { 322 translate: 0; 323 } 324 } 325 ``` 326 327 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 328 329 #### Anchoring the header 330 331 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 332 333 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 334 335 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 336
337 {/* navigation links */} 338
339 ``` 340 341 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 342 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 343 animation: none; 344 z-index: 100; 345 } 346 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 347 display: none; 348 } 349 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 350 animation: none; 351 } 352 ``` 353 354 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 355 356 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 357 358 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 359 360 #### Keeping the page interactive 361 362 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 363 364 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 365 ::view-transition { 366 pointer-events: none; 367 } 368 ``` 369 370 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 371 372 #### Respecting reduced motion 373 374 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 375 376 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 377 378 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 379 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 380 ::view-transition-old(*), 381 ::view-transition-new(*), 382 ::view-transition-group(*) { 383 animation-duration: 0s !important; 384 animation-delay: 0s !important; 385 } 386 } 387 ``` 388 389 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 390 391 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 392 393 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 394 395 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 396 397 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 398 399 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 400 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 401 402 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 403 const { slug } = await params 404 405 return ( 406 }> 407 414 415 416 417 ) 418 } 419 ``` 420 421 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 422 423 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 424 425 ## Next steps 426 427 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location. 428 429 Each pattern answers a different question for the user: 430 431 | Pattern | What it communicates | 432 | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | 433 | Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper" | 434 | Suspense reveal | "Data loaded" | 435 | Directional slide | "Going forward / coming back" | 436 | Same-route crossfade | "Same place, different content" | 437 438 For API details and more patterns: 439 440 - [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes) 441 - [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router), which also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()` 442 - [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) 443 - [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file 444

content.text:
View transitions are in place and verified end-to-end in a headless Chromium against a production build: the thumbnail-to-hero morph, directional page slides, Suspense skeleton-to-content reveals, and reduced-motion handling all fire as intended.

## What changed

No new dependencies or config were needed. This Next.js 16.4 canary ships a React canary that exports `ViewTransition` from `react`, `@types/react` 19.3 already types it, and `<Link>` accepts a `transitionTypes` prop.

**`app/PageTransition.tsx` (new)** — a small wrapper around `<ViewTransition>` that maps the `nav-forward` / `nav-back` transition types to CSS classes and uses `default: 'none'` so untyped transitions (browser back button, refresh, Suspense reveals) don't slide. It wraps each page's content rather than the layout, because layouts persist across navigations and would never fire enter/exit.

**`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — each thumbnail is wrapped in `<ViewTransition name="product-image-{slug}" share="morph" default="none">`, and each card's `<Link>` carries `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`.

**`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — the hero gets the same `name` as its thumbnail so React pairs them and the browser morphs between them. The back link carries `nav-back`. The Suspense fallback is wrapped with `exit="slide-down"` and the async details with `enter="slide-up"`. I also changed the outer `<div>` to `<main>` so the detail page picks up the same max-width/padding as the grid page; the slide reads oddly if the two pages have different horizontal alignment.

**`app/page.tsx`** — same page wrapper and Suspense reveal treatment as the detail page.

**`app/globals.css`** — the animation definitions: a 400ms morph with a mid-flight blur to hide interpolation artifacts; asymmetric Suspense timing (150ms skeleton exit, then a delayed 210ms fade-in with a longer 400ms upward slide); ±60px horizontal slides for forward/back; `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` so clicks aren't swallowed mid-animation; and a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block.

## Reduced motion

Rather than zeroing everything, the reduced-motion block removes all positional movement and blur but keeps short opacity fades, so state changes remain legible: page slides and Suspense reveals become plain crossfades, the morph snaps to its final position and crossfades in place, and the skeleton pulse becomes static.

One thing worth knowing about, since it's easy to get wrong: my first attempt used `animation: none` on the morph's `::view-transition-group`, which silently turned the morph into an instant swap. In Chromium the old/new snapshot pseudo-elements inherit `animation-duration` from the group, so the shorthand zeroed their crossfade too. Using `animation-name: none` instead keeps the crossfade; there's a comment in the CSS explaining this.

## Verification

Playwright drove a `next build` + `next start` instance, intercepting `document.startViewTransition` to record transition types, which elements carried a `view-transition-name` in the old and new DOM, and which keyframes ran on the `::view-transition-*` pseudo-elements. With motion enabled: forward navigation carried `nav-forward`, the clicked thumbnail and the destination hero shared the name `product-image-leather-backpack`, `via-blur` and `slide-x` ran, and the untyped Suspense reveal ran the `slide-y` exit and enter. With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: no `slide-x`, `slide-y`, or `via-blur` ran, only `fade-only` plus the browser's crossfade. A frozen mid-transition screenshot showed the thumbnail visibly in flight toward the hero slot. `tsc --noEmit` and `next build` both pass.

Two notes: the `package.json` and `package-lock.json` modifications in `git status` were already present before I started and aren't mine. And browser-initiated back navigation (the back button) carries no transition type, so it gets the morph but not the directional slide; that's inherent to the API, not something the app can tag.
